extracted.intended_audience: educated lay readers and naturalists (general public interested in natural history and practical safety)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing evidence and functional explanations for how fruit and seed structures serve dispersal and establishment (e.g., by animals, wind, hygroscopic burial). Includes practical guidance on human drowning-avoidance behavior presented later in the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colored fleshy fruits attract animals
rubrics_metrics.description: In a very large number of cases the diffusion of seeds is effected by animals. In them an outer fleshy portion becomes pulpy, and generally sweet, inclosing the seeds. It is remarkable that such fruits, in order, doubtless, to attract animals, are, like flowers, brightly colored — as, for instance, the cherry, currant, apple, peach, plum, strawberry, raspberry, and many others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color develops at maturity (not present in unripe fruit) and thus signals ripeness; the actual seed is generally protected by a dense, sometimes almost stony, covering so that it escapes digestion, while its germination is perhaps hastened by the heat of the animal's body. Examples: cherry, currant, apple, peach, plum, strawberry, raspberry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edible seeds protected by hard or bitter envelopes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the seeds themselves are edible they are generally protected by more or less hard or bitter envelopes, for instance the horse-chestnut, beech, Spanish chestnut, walnut, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of such seeds by animals is not necessarily harmful to the plant because animals may carry and drop or store and forget them, carrying seeds away from the parent tree—this can promote dispersal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruits with hooks for epizoochory (attachment to animals)
rubrics_metrics.description: In another class of instances animals, unconsciously or unwillingly, serve in the dispersion of seeds. These cases may be divided into two classes, those in which the fruits are provided with hooks, and those in which they are sticky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples among English plants: burdock (Lappa), agrimony (Agrimonia), bur parsley (Caucalis), enchanter's nightshade (Circaea), cleavers (Galium), some forget-me-nots (Myosotis). Foreign species with formidable hooks: Martynia proboscidea, Harpagophytum procumbens. Note arrangement of hooks promotes removal of fruits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sticky/viscid fruits for adhesion-mediated dispersal
rubrics_metrics.description: The cases in which the diffusion of fruits and seeds is affected by their being sticky are less numerous... The common plumbago of South Europe is a case. Other genera: Pittosporum, Pisonia, Boerhavia, Sigesbeckia, Grubelia, Drymaria, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sticky mucilage can make seeds adhere to bark (useful for mistletoe and Arceuthobium) or to birds/animals, aiding dispersal and establishment on suitable substrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dispersal mechanisms in one species
rubrics_metrics.description: There are comparatively few cases in which the same plant uses more than one of these modes of promoting the dispersion of its seeds, still there are some such instances. Thus in the common burdock the seeds have a pappus, while the whole flower-head is provided with hooks which readily attach themselves to any passing animal. Asterothrix has three provisions for dispersion; it has a hollow appendage, a pappus, and a rough surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a single species may combine wind, attachment, and other methods to maximize dispersal opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional/habitual evidence supports adaptive function
rubrics_metrics.description: If the wing was accidental ... We should naturally expect to find some species with hooks in all classes of plants. ... Now, such a fruit would be of little use to low herbs... I find thirty genera, belonging to twenty-one different natural orders, figured as having seeds or fruits of this form. They are all trees or climbing shrubs, not one being a low herb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ecological/taxonomic distribution of a trait (e.g., winged fruits occur predominantly on trees and climbing shrubs, not low herbs) as evidence that the trait is adaptive for the particular life-form rather than accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait occurrence must be consistent with the dispersal agent's ecology
rubrics_metrics.description: We have about thirty English species in which the dispersion of the seeds is effected by means of hooks, but not one of these is aquatic, nor is one of them more than four feet high. ... It would also seem ... that in point of time, also, the appearance of the families of plants in which the fruits or seeds are provided with hooks coincided with that of the land mammalia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the presence/absence of a trait matches the ecology/behavior/size/habitat of the proposed dispersal agents (e.g., hooked seeds associated with low terrestrial plants where mammal fur contact is likely). Temporal correlation with the appearance of the agent strengthens the adaptive inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional morphology matching hypothesized role
rubrics_metrics.description: The hooks, moreover, are so arranged as to promote the removal of the fruits. ... The long feather [on Stipa pennata], no doubt, facilitates the dispersion of the seeds by wind; eventually, however, they sink to the ground, which they tend to reach; the seeds being the heaviest portion, point downward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the detailed form and mechanics of the structure (hooks, wings, pappus, appendages, spiral awns) plausibly perform the postulated dispersal or burial function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental and observational demonstration of mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: His observations were made on an allied species, Erodium cicutarium, ... if a seed of this plant is laid on the ground, it remains quiet as long as it is dry; but as soon as it is moistened ... the outer side of the awn contracts, and the hairs surrounding the seed commence to move outward, the result of which is gradually to raise the seed into an upright position with its point on the soil. The awn then commences to unroll ... and will therefore tend to drive the seed into the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, seek experimental or repeatable observational evidence of the mechanism (hygroscopic awn motion burying seeds, wind or animal transport observations, sticky mucilage adhesion). Examples: Roux on awns; Vaucher/Frank Darwin on Stipa; Hooker on Myzodendron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed size/number tailored to establishment niche
rubrics_metrics.description: In many epiphytes the seeds are extremely numerous and minute. Their great numbers increase the chance that the wind may waft some of them to the trees on which they grow; and as they are then fully supplied with nourishment they do not require to carry any store with them. Moreover, their minute size is an advantage, as they are carried into any little chink or cranny in the bark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret seed size and fecundity in light of the target germination substrate—tiny numerous seeds for epiphytes, fewer/larger seeds for subterranean pods where competition would be harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterocarpy / production of multiple seed types for different strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Heterocarpism ... or the power of producing two kinds of reproductive bodies, is not confined to these species. ... in C. chenopodifolium, besides the usual long pods, produces also short, pointed ones, which it buries in the ground. ... the subterranean pods differ from the usual aerial form in being shorter and containing fewer seeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize dual strategies (some seeds adapted to local burial/establishment, others to broader dispersal); differences in size/number reflect trade-offs between dispersal range and local avoidance of sibling competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms that actively bury seeds (hygroscopic/elastic devices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of spiral turns in the awn depends upon the amount of moisture; and the seed may thus be made into a very delicate hygrometer... the seed may be gradually driven into the ground by the awn's movement. ... In Stipa pennata the posterior end of the seed is produced into a fine twisted corkscrew-like rod ... if a shower comes on, or when the dew falls, the spiral unwinds ... the seed itself is forced down and so driven by degrees into the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for hygroscopic, elastic, or mechanical structures (awn twisting/unwinding, corkscrew rods, reversed hairs) whose cyclical response to moisture/heat accomplishes burial without animal assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching fruit/seed position and structure to germination site
rubrics_metrics.description: The next point is that seeds should be in a spot suitable for their growth. In most cases the seed lies on the ground, into which it then pushes its little rootlet. In plants which live on trees, the case is not so simple, and we meet some curious contrivances. Thus, the mistletoe ... is extremely sticky and thus adheres to the bark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the dispersal mechanism places seeds where they can establish (e.g., sticky seeds adhering to branches for mistletoe; appendages that catch on bark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological mimicry may influence interactions with animals
rubrics_metrics.description: The seeds of Abrus precatorius, both in size and in their very striking color, mimic a small beetle, Artemis circumnista. ... Martynia, Lupins, Dimorphiochlamys, castor-oil seeds, Jatropha ... resemble insects or beetles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesize possible adaptive consequences of seed mimicry (attracting birds to swallow seeds; or deterring granivorous birds by appearing as insects). Note experiments or natural-history observations are needed to determine the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against inferring function from single cases; need broad comparative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: But perhaps it will be said that I have picked out special cases; that others could have been selected, which would not bear out, or perhaps would even negative, the inferences which have been indicated; that I have put the cart before the horse ... doubtless there are many points connected with seeds which are still unexplained; in fact, it is because this is so that I was anxious to direct attention to the subject. Still I believe the general explanations which have been given by botanists will stand any test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on isolated examples; seek comprehensive comparisons across taxa, habits, and life-forms to support adaptive explanations. Acknowledge uncertainties and remaining questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tread/walk the water as drowning-avoidance technique
rubrics_metrics.description: When one of the inferior animals takes the water, falls or is thrown in, it instantly begins to walk as it does when out of the water. But, when a man who cannot 'swim' falls into the water, he makes a few spasmodic struggles, throws up his arms, and drowns. ... In order, then, to escape drowning, it is only necessary to do as the brute does, and that is to tread or walk the water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate quadruped movement: remain calm, and move limbs in alternating rhythm (one two, one two) without hurry or precipitation. This 'walking' keeps the body buoyant and avoids energy-wasting spasms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spasmodic struggles; maintain calm steady motions
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who wishes to save his life, and can not otherwise swim, must do so too, striking alternately, one two, one two, but without hurry or precipitation, with hand and foot, exactly as the brute does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep slow, steady alternating strokes with hands and feet; use the paddle-like hand surface; resist panic. Any person who can walk on land can 'walk' in water this way without prior instruction.
